h1: She asked for Robux to learn about money. Her dad said yes.
sub: For a year the answer was no. At eight, she changed her pitch.
lines: P	Short answer: Buying your kid Robux can be a cheap, low-stakes money lesson if you set the cap in dollars and talk about every purchase. Two things make it harder than it looks: Robux hide the real price, and many Roblox games sell paid shortcuts. Saying no is a fine answer too.
H2	The pitch

P	One of my coworkers at EKUZO, where we coach kids' gaming teams, has an 8-year-old daughter. She's played Roblox for about a year, mostly Dress to Impress: you get a theme, a few minutes to put an outfit together, then you walk a runway and the other players vote.

P	The whole time, she asked for Robux, Roblox's currency, so she can buy VIP. For a year, her parents always said no. Her dad's blunt about why: the game has casino elements, and it's fine if she has fun, but he won't support spending for shortcuts.
P	Then she turned eight and changed her argument. In her words, “dad, I need to learn about money at some point, and this is a good place to do it.”

P	Her dad, impressed and a little surprised, decided to meet her where she is. He said yes, then he set his own goals: teach her how money works, how to think about priorities, and the discipline to make it last.
H2	Why he said yes
P	His reason was about control.
P	“A game is a safe place. As long as I put the limit and the safety in place, it's actually a great testing zone.”

P	He set the amount, $20, and he can see everything she does with it. He called it a pilot. And he was thinking past the game: someday she'll have an allowance, and it will go to food, going out with friends and buying gifts. He equated it to a practice round.
H2	How the conversation changed
P	Before, when she asked he said no, and that was the whole conversation.

P	Now it's one they both want to have. She gets to talk about the thing she cares about: the outfits, the runway, and what else she's considering. He gets to talk about the thing he cares about: what something costs, what's worth spending on, and what she'll do when it's gone.
P	“I get to be in her world, and have her be in mine. Meeting in the middle has changed how we talk about it.”
P	That's the line I keep coming back to. My mom didn't get behind my gaming until it had earned me a scholarship. When she finally told me to go train, I cried.
H2	What her $20 actually buys

P	Robux hide the price. On the web, $9.99 buys 1,000 Robux (a $10 gift card gets the same), so her $20 is roughly 2,000. Inside the mobile app, the same money buys fewer. Researchers at the University of Sydney who interviewed children about Roblox found they struggled to work out what Robux cost in real money. So say the dollars out loud, and compare it to other things in the real world.

P	VIP in Dress to Impress buys clothes and a room. The permanent pass is 799 Robux in the game's store, roughly $8 at the web rate, which would be about 40% of her $20. It unlocks a VIP room with VIP-only clothing and accessories. It doesn't buy rank. Ranks, and the harder lobbies, come from the stars other players give you on the runway. A kid can believe VIP is how you get to the top, so it's a good first question to ask together: what does this get you?

P	The game will offer more. Running faster, more items per outfit, double in-game money, each sold as its own pass. Each one is small. The lesson is deciding before the store opens, and getting ahead of the casino elements.
H2	What she did with it
P	She spent about $3 on an outfit. The free avatar has almost no style, and she wanted something that was hers, though not the rarest look in the store, because they talked about it.
P	Plenty of players wear what she picked: long hair, a pink T-shirt and a skirt. It looks a little like her. It didn't need to be flashy, but it's hers.
P	Then she bought VIP in Dress to Impress, the one-time permanent pass. The VIP room in the game she plays most is now open to her.
P	That left roughly half her money. She has her eye on a few things but hasn't picked one yet.
H2	If you're thinking about it
LI	Pick the amount in dollars before you open the app.

LI	Link a parent account to your kid's and turn on activity and spending notifications. Roblox sends activity updates and a notice when money is spent. A monthly spending limit doesn't cover gift card redemptions, so if you use a gift card, the card is the limit. Check which account type your kid has, too: Roblox's accounts start very restrictive for ages 5-8 (including limiting games that show up), then slowly progress with more responsibilities.
LI	Convert out loud, every time. Robux to dollars needs to be understood. Ideally give comparisons to other things in their life.
LI	Ask what they get for their purchase before they buy it and have a real conversation.
LI	Agree in advance what happens when it's gone. (The answer that teaches the most is: it's gone.)
LI	Regularly talk about it. That's the part you're paying for.
H2	What I'd keep in mind
P	Roblox isn't a neutral place to run this experiment.

LI	Safety is a live issue. Since 2025, several state attorneys general, including Texas's, have sued Roblox over child safety, and others, including West Virginia and Kansas, have reached settlements requiring safety changes. Roblox has added an age check to chat (January 2026) and, in June 2026, separate accounts for kids 5 to 8 with chat off by default and a narrower catalog. While helpful, none of that replaces a parent who knows who their kid is talking to.

LI	The design pushes. Advocacy groups filed an FTC complaint in May 2026 arguing that Roblox's currency and scarcity tactics manipulate kids. Roblox says it builds “for fun and connection, not short-term engagement.” Either way, your kid is shopping in a store built to sell to them.
P	I won't pretend one $20 pilot makes an eight-year-old good with money. What's different is that they're willing to talk about it on the same side of the table.
P	Weighing a ban instead? Here's how one family handled Fortnite. For the bigger picture, read what your kid's gaming is telling you, or ask one of our coaches.
H2	Common questions
H3	Is Roblox safe for younger kids?

P	It depends on the settings and on you. Since June 2026, Roblox places kids 5 to 8 in accounts with chat off by default and a narrower set of games, and a linked parent account can control spending, screen time and who your kid can talk to. Several states are suing Roblox over child safety. Turn the controls on, pay attention, and check in.
H3	How much is VIP in Dress to Impress?
P	The game's store lists 799 Robux for the permanent pass and 299 Robux for 30 days, roughly $8 and $3 at web or gift-card rates. Prices change, so check the in-game store.
H3	Does VIP help you rank up in Dress to Impress?
P	No. VIP unlocks a VIP room with exclusive clothes and accessories. Ranks come from the stars other players vote on the runway.
H3	How do I use Roblox parental controls to limit spending?

P	Link a parent account to your kid's account, then load or set a monthly spending limit with notifications on. Gift card redemptions don't count toward the limit. If you just connect an account, the default is no limit. And if you set a limit, Roblox doesn't tell you when they reach it. The default spending alerts start at $100 a month, so set notifications to every transaction.
H3	How much real money is a Robux?

P	On the web, $9.99 buys 1,000 Robux (a $10 gift card gets the same), so about a penny each. In-app purchases usually give fewer Robux for the same money; it's almost always better to buy and load for them, vs let them buy in the app.

imgs.alt: A dad and his daughter at the kitchen counter, looking at a Dress to Impress runway on her tablet; he points to the five stars other players gave her outfit.

One game, two things to talk about. She talks about the outfit she's saving for, winning the runway, what's new in the store, and what she'll buy first. Dad talks about what it costs in real dollars, what it actually gets you, what happens when it's gone, and whether it's worth the wait. One conversation they both want.
